stem: Why is Prometheus a poor choice for per-request customer billing?

options.text: It isn't designed for 100% accuracy, so the data won't be detailed and complete enough
options.note: Right. The overview names billing as the example of when Prometheus doesn't fit.

options.text: It can't store integers
options.note: Values are float64, which is exact for integers up to 2^53. Precision isn't the main issue.

options.text: It can only keep data for 24 hours
options.note: Default retention is 15 days, and it's configurable.

options.text: It has no query language
options.note: PromQL is very capable. The problem is completeness of the data.

explanation: If you need 100% accuracy, such as for per-request billing, Prometheus isn't a good choice, because the collected data won't be detailed and complete enough.
hint: What does reliability-first monitoring trade away?

sources.title: Overview › When does it not fit?

stem: Someone asks how to feed application logs into Prometheus. What do the docs answer?

options.text: Don't. Use a log system such as Grafana Loki or OpenSearch instead
options.note: Right. Prometheus collects metrics. It isn't an event logging system.

options.text: Send them through the Pushgateway
options.note: The Pushgateway is for batch job metrics, not logs.

options.text: Expose each log line as a label value
options.note: That would explode cardinality and still isn't a log store.

options.text: Use remote write
options.note: Remote write ships samples, not logs.

explanation: The FAQ's short answer is "Don't!". Use something like Grafana Loki or OpenSearch. Prometheus is a system to collect and process metrics, not an event logging system.
hint: The FAQ answer is one word long.

sources.title: FAQ › How to feed logs into Prometheus?

stem: Which statement about Prometheus local storage is correct?

options.text: It isn't clustered or replicated, so it should be managed like a single-node database
options.note: Right. That's the main limitation of local storage.

options.text: It automatically replicates data to all other Prometheus servers
options.note: There's no replication between servers.

options.text: It's a distributed database across all scrape targets
options.note: Data lives only on the server's local disk.

options.text: It requires NFS for durability
options.note: NFS (including AWS EFS) isn't supported. Use a local filesystem.

explanation: A limitation of local storage is that it isn't clustered or replicated, so it isn't arbitrarily scalable or durable against drive or node outages and should be managed like any single-node database.
hint: Where is the data physically stored?

stem: If neither retention flag is set, how long does Prometheus keep samples?

options.text: 15 days
options.note: Right. --storage.tsdb.retention.time defaults to 15d when no retention is configured.

options.text: Forever
options.note: There's a default time-based retention.

options.text: 24 hours
options.note: That's much shorter than the default.

options.text: 1 year
options.note: The default is 15 days.

explanation: If neither --storage.tsdb.retention.time nor --storage.tsdb.retention.size is set, retention time defaults to 15d.

stem: You need to keep metrics for several years with durability. What's the usual approach?

options.text: Use remote write to send samples to an external long-term storage system
options.note: Right. External storage through remote read/write is the documented route.

options.text: Set retention to 5 years on a single server and rely on it
options.note: Possible in theory, but local storage isn't replicated or durable against node failure.

options.text: Push everything through the Pushgateway
options.note: The Pushgateway isn't a storage system.

options.text: Increase scrape_interval to 1 hour
options.note: That reduces resolution. It doesn't give durability.

explanation: External storage may be used via the remote read/write APIs. These systems vary greatly in durability, performance and efficiency.
hint: Prometheus can send its samples elsewhere as they arrive.

stem: How do the docs say to make Prometheus highly available?

options.text: Run identical Prometheus servers on two or more separate machines
options.note: Right. Deduplicate downstream, and Alertmanager deduplicates identical alerts.

options.text: Enable built-in clustering with --cluster.peer
options.note: The Prometheus server has no built-in clustering. That flag belongs to Alertmanager's HA.

options.text: Put Prometheus behind a load balancer with shared NFS storage
options.note: NFS isn't supported for local storage, and that isn't the documented approach.

options.text: It can't be made highly available
options.note: It can, by running identical servers.

explanation: Run identical Prometheus servers on two or more separate machines. Systems like Thanos, or remote-write backends, can deduplicate the data. Identical alerts are deduplicated by Alertmanager.

sources.title: FAQ › Can Prometheus be made highly available?

stem: Two identical Prometheus servers both fire the same alert. What stops on-call engineers getting two notifications?

options.text: Alertmanager deduplicates identical alerts
options.note: Right. That's part of the HA story in the FAQ.

options.text: The second Prometheus detects the first and stays silent
options.note: The servers are independent and don't coordinate.

options.text: The Pushgateway merges them
options.note: The Pushgateway isn't involved in alerting.

options.text: Nothing. Duplicate pages are expected with HA
options.note: Alertmanager handles the deduplication.

explanation: In the HA setup, identical alerts from the redundant servers are deduplicated by Alertmanager, which can itself be clustered for HA.
hint: Which component sits between alerts and notifications?

sources.title: FAQ › Can Prometheus be made highly available?

stem: What's the most common practical cause of a Prometheus server running out of resources?

options.text: A cardinality explosion from labels with unbounded values
options.note: Right. Each label combination is a new series with RAM, CPU and disk costs.

options.text: Too many PromQL functions in one query
options.note: Complex queries cost CPU, but unbounded series growth is the classic resource killer.

options.text: Using the text exposition format
options.note: The format choice doesn't cause resource exhaustion.

options.text: Having more than five scrape jobs
options.note: Prometheus handles many jobs easily. Series count matters far more.

explanation: Each labelset is an additional series with RAM, CPU, disk and network costs. Unbounded label values such as per-user labels can push a server into millions of series, which is too much.

sources.title: FAQ › I was told Prometheus “doesn't scale”

stem: Roughly how many active series do the docs say a single Prometheus server can run reliably?

options.text: Tens of millions
options.note: Right. The FAQ says you can run Prometheus reliably with tens of millions of active series.

options.text: A few thousand
options.note: That's far below what a single server can handle.

options.text: Exactly 1 million, a hard limit
options.note: There's no such hard limit.

options.text: Unlimited, because cardinality never matters
options.note: Cardinality matters a lot. There are practical limits.

explanation: The FAQ calls "Prometheus doesn't scale" more of a marketing claim and says you can run Prometheus reliably with tens of millions of active series.
hint: The FAQ addresses this claim directly.

sources.title: FAQ › I was told Prometheus “doesn't scale”

stem: Sample values are 64-bit floats. Up to what size are integers represented exactly?

options.note: Right. IEEE 754 doubles are integer-exact up to 2^53.
Doubles go well beyond that.
That's the 64-bit integer limit. Floats are exact only to 2^53.

options.text: Any size
options.note: Beyond 2^53, not all integers can be represented exactly.

explanation: The IEEE 754 double-precision format supports integer precision for values up to 2^53. A counter incremented a million times per second would take over 285 years to hit precision issues.

sources.title: FAQ › Why are all sample values 64-bit floats?

stem: Why do Prometheus components display times in UTC?

options.text: To avoid timezone confusion, especially around daylight saving time
options.note: Right. Unix time internally and UTC for display.

options.text: Because Prometheus can't store timezone data
options.note: It's a deliberate design choice to avoid confusion.

options.text: Because the CNCF requires it
options.note: That isn't the reason given in the FAQ.

options.text: Because scrapes only happen at midnight UTC
options.note: Scrapes happen continuously.

explanation: To avoid any kind of timezone confusion, especially with daylight saving time, Prometheus uses Unix time internally and UTC for display in all components.
hint: Think about clocks changing twice a year.

sources.title: FAQ › Why is everything in UTC?

stem: According to the comparison page, when is Prometheus the better fit?

options.text: When you're primarily doing metrics and want strong querying, alerting and availability
options.note: Right. That's how the docs describe where Prometheus wins.

options.text: When you're primarily doing event logging
options.note: The docs say event-logging-oriented systems fit that better.

options.text: When you need a clustered long-term store as the core requirement
options.note: Clustered long-term storage isn't Prometheus's built-in strength.

options.text: When you need per-transaction billing data
options.note: That needs 100% accuracy, which Prometheus doesn't aim for.

explanation: The comparison page says Prometheus is better if you're primarily doing metrics, with a more powerful query language, alerting and notification, and higher availability for graphing and alerting.
